source_text:
Κατανοήσωμεν, ἀγαπητοί, πῶς ὁ δεσπότης ἐπιδείκνυται διηνεκῶς ἡμῖν τὴν μέλλουσαν ἀνάστασιν ἔσεσθαι, ἧς τὴν ἀπαρχὴν ἐποιήσατο τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστήσας.
ἴδωμεν, ἀγαπητοί. τὴν κατὰ καιρὸν γινομένην ἀνάστασιν.
ἡμέρα καὶ νὺξ ἀνάστασιν ἡμῖν δηλοῦσιν: κοιμᾶται ἡ νύξ, ἀνίσταται ἡ ἡμέρα: ἡ ἡμέρα ἄπεισιν, νὺξ ἐπέρχεται.
λάβωμεν τοὺς καρπούς: ὁ σπόρος πῶς καὶ τίνα τρόπον γίνεται;
ἐξῆλθεν ὁ σπείρων καὶ ἔβαλεν εἰς τὴν γῆν ἕκαστον τῶν σπερμάτων, ἅτινα πεσόντα εἰς τὴν γῆν ξηρὰ καὶ γυμνὰ διαλύεται: εἶτ̓ ἐκ τῆς διαλύσεως ἡ μεγαλειότης τῆς προνοίας τοῦ δεσπότου ἀνίστησιν αὐτά, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς πλείονα αὔξει καὶ ἐκφέρει καρπόν.
thought_title: Nature's daily and yearly resurrections foreshadow the future resurrection
orientation: The Roman church, addressing the Corinthians as 'beloved,' is beginning a series of examples from the natural world to show that God constantly demonstrates the future resurrection.
pass_a_gloss: Let us consider, beloved, how the Master continuously shows us the resurrection that is about to be, of which he made the firstfruits the Lord Jesus Christ, having raised him from the dead. Let us see, beloved, the resurrection that happens according to season. Day and night show us a resurrection: the night sleeps, the day rises: the day departs, night comes on. Let us take the fruits: the seed, how and in what manner does it come to be? The sower went out and cast into the earth each of the seeds, which, having fallen into the earth, dry and bare, dissolve: then from the dissolution the majesty of the providence of the Master raises them up, and from the one increases more and brings forth fruit.

choices.why: The term denotes God as sovereign owner and lord; 'Master' preserves the authority and ownership implied, distinct from 'Lord' used for Christ in the same passage.

choices.english: the resurrection that is about to be
choices.why: The future infinitive with μέλλουσαν emphasizes the certainty and imminence of the coming resurrection; the rendering keeps the future-oriented force.

choices.english: of which he made the firstfruits
choices.why: The middle voice ἐποιήσατο indicates God made Christ the firstfruits for himself; 'made the firstfruits' preserves the middle force and the agricultural metaphor.
rejected: of which he made a first offering

choices.term: ἡμέρα καὶ νὺξ ἀνάστασιν ἡμῖν δηλοῦσιν
choices.english: Day and night show us a resurrection
choices.why: The present tense δηλοῦσιν indicates an ongoing, continuous demonstration; 'show us' keeps the dative of advantage and the present force.
rejected: Day and night declare to us a resurrection
Day and night reveal a resurrection to us

choices.term: ἡ μεγαλειότης τῆς προνοίας τοῦ δεσπότου
choices.english: the majesty of the providence of the Master
choices.why: The genitive chain is kept literal to preserve the theological weight: the majesty belongs to the providence, which belongs to the Master.
rejected: the majestic providence of the Master
the greatness of the Master's providence

choices.why: The literal 'from the one' preserves the contrast between the single seed and the many that result; 'increases more' keeps the comparative force of πλείονα.

bible_refs.note: Christ as firstfruits of the resurrection (ἀπαρχὴ) echoes Paul's language, though Clement's wording is his own.

pass_b_english: Let us consider, beloved, how the Master continually shows us that the resurrection is about to be. He made the Lord Jesus Christ its firstfruits by raising him from the dead.
Let us look, beloved, at the resurrection that happens in its season.
Day and night show us a resurrection. Night sleeps, and day rises. Day departs, and night comes on.
Let us take the fruits. How does the seed come about, and in what manner?

The sower went out and cast each of the seeds into the ground. They fall into the ground dry and bare, and they dissolve. Then from their dissolution the majesty of the Master's providence raises them up, and from the one seed he increases more and brings forth fruit.

polish.changed: Clarified sentence rhythm and pronoun references, made the day and night sequence easier to follow aloud, and specified that the Master's providence raises the seeds and increases fruit from the one seed.

last_rejected.source_quote: κοιμᾶται ἡ νύξ, ἀνίσταται ἡ ἡμέρα
last_rejected.why: Greek says night sleeps/falls, day rises; English inverts to night sleeps, day rises—actually correct. Wait: κοιμᾶται is middle/passive 'lies down, sleeps'; ἀνίσταται 'rises'. English has night sleeps, day rises. This matches.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'night sleeps, day rises' correctly renders κοιμᾶται ἡ νύξ, ἀνίσταται ἡ ἡμέρα; no inversion or error.

last_rejected.quote: from their dissolution the majesty of the providence of the Master raises them up
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐκ τῆς διαλύσεως ἡ μεγαλειότης τῆς προνοίας τοῦ δεσπότου ἀνίστησιν αὐτά
last_rejected.why: Greek says 'the majesty of the providence of the Master raises them'; English adds 'from their dissolution' as if dissolution is agent, but ἐκ means 'out of/from' dissolution as source, not agent. English 'from their dissolution... raises them up' is slightly ambiguous but conveys 'out of dissolution' correctly.
last_rejected.fix: out of their dissolution the majesty of the Master's providence raises them
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκ τῆς διαλύσεως means 'from/out of dissolution'; English 'from their dissolution...raises' correctly conveys source, not agency.

last_rejected.quote: from the one increases more and brings forth fruit
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς πλείονα αὔξει καὶ ἐκφέρει καρπόν
last_rejected.why: Subject is 'the majesty of the providence' from prior clause; English lacks explicit subject, making 'from the one increases more' ungrammatical/readable. 'from the one' should be 'from the one [seed] it increases more [seeds]'
last_rejected.fix: and from the one it increases to more and brings forth fruit
last_rejected.ruling: Subject carries over from prior clause; 'from the one increases more' is awkward but intelligible, within acceptable range.

last_rejected.quote: and from the one seed he increases more and brings forth fruit.
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς πλείονα αὔξει καὶ ἐκφέρει καρπόν.
last_rejected.why: πλείονα is the subject: many grow from the one and bear fruit. English makes the Master increase and bear fruit, and loses “many.”
last_rejected.fix: and from the one seed many grow and bring forth fruit.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'from the one seed he increases more' keeps 'more' (πλείονα) as object of αὔξει; plausible reading, 'increases... brings forth fruit' within range; 'many' not lost.
